reason: The text exemplifies good leadership through Nehemiah's response to social-economic injustices. Nehemiah identifies exploitation by nobles and officials (taking interest, enslaving people, mortgaging property), publicly rebukes these practices, demands restitution, and implements reforms. The passage explicitly contrasts bad leadership (previous governors who 'burdened the people, took money and provisions' through their servants) with Nehemiah's model of good governance: he refuses the governor's rations to 'lighten the burden on the people,' dedicates himself to communal work (the wall), and provides hospitality without demanding payment. His actions are motivated 'by fear of God.' The text presents this as the standard of leadership worth remembering—functioning government explicitly oriented toward the people's welfare rather than exploitation.
